chapters.title: Case Endings and Dative Subjects
chapters.label: ch:te-dative-case
chapters.canDo: I can say that I know Telugu the way Telugu itself says it — "to me Telugu comes," with no subject and the dative -ku.

payoff.summary: Say నాకు తెలుగు వచ్చు against నేను తెలుగు మాట్లాడతాను, then line up the four Dravidian datives -ku · -ukku · -ge · -ikku.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Ten
chapters.label: ch:te-numbers-one-to-ten
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to ten in Telugu, including the numbers that wander furthest from their Dravidian cousins.

payoff.summary: Count ఒకటి through పది, say the two Telugu builds fresh — enimidi and tommidi — and hear seven's three fates in ēḻu, ēḷu and ēḍu.

chapters.title: Please
chapters.label: ch:te-please
chapters.canDo: I can say please in Telugu, and use the polite -aṇḍi verb ending speakers actually reach for.

payoff.summary: Build దయచేసి out of daya ("compassion") + cēsi ("having done"), then make the everyday polite request instead: కూర్చోండి, "please sit."

chapters.title: Sorry
chapters.label: ch:te-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Telugu and ask someone to forgive me, using the same respectful ending.

payoff.summary: Say క్షమించండి, unpack it as kṣamin̄cu plus the respectful -aṇḍi already met in kūrcōṇḍi, and trace it to Sanskrit kṣamā.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:te-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name any day of the week in Telugu, including the Sunday that is counted rather than named for a planet.

payoff.summary: Run Somavāram through Śanivāram, then name Sunday ఆదివారం, "the first day" — positional like Arabic's numbered days, not planetary.

chapters.title: Four Core Colours
chapters.label: ch:te-core-colours
chapters.canDo: I can name four basic colours in Telugu — black, white, red, and blue.

payoff.summary: Say నలుపు, తెలుపు, ఎరుపు — Telugu's own three — then నీలం, blue, which Telugu borrowed rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.label: ch:te-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my parents and my brothers and sisters in Telugu, choosing the right word for older or younger.

payoff.summary: Name నాన్న and అమ్మ, then the four age-graded siblings అన్న · తమ్ముడు · అక్క · చెల్లి, with చెల్లి being Telugu's own.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:te-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say తల, plainly matching its cousins, and చెయ్యి — the same Dravidian root as kai, reshaped by sound change past easy recognition.

chapters.title: Seasons
chapters.label: ch:te-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name the four seasons in Telugu, including the rains that anchor the year.

payoff.summary: Say వేసవి (cousin of Kannada's bēsige), వానాకాలం and శీతాకాలం from native roots, then the doubly-Sanskrit వసంత ఋతువు.

chapters.title: Water and Rice
chapters.label: ch:te-water-and-rice
chapters.canDo: I can ask for water in Telugu and tell raw rice apart from cooked rice.

payoff.summary: Say నీళ్ళు — matching Tamil and Kannada — then separate బియ్యం, Telugu's own word for raw rice, from అన్నం, the cooked rice on the plate.

chapters.title: The Traditional Months
chapters.label: ch:te-traditional-months
chapters.canDo: I can name the twelve traditional Telugu months and say when Ugadi, the new year, falls.

payoff.summary: Recite Caitraṁ through Phālguṇaṁ, place Ugadi at Chaitra Śuddha Pādyami, and note the family split: Telugu and Kannada share Hindi's calendar, Tamil and Malayalam do not.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:te-noon-and-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say noon and midnight in Telugu and explain why one is "middle" and the other "half."

payoff.summary: Say మధ్యాహ్నం and అర్ధరాత్రి, then separate madhya ("middle") from ardha ("half") — two different Sanskrit roots where Kannada uses one.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:te-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can tell someone the time on the hour in Telugu, in the singular and the plural.

payoff.summary: Say గంట — hour, and also "bell" — then ఒక గంట for one o'clock and రెండు గంటలు for two, taking the plural -lu.

chapters.title: Asking Someone's Age
chapters.label: ch:te-asking-age
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone how old they are in Telugu and give my own age in return.

payoff.summary: Ask నీ వయసెంత? and answer నా వయసు ఇరవై — a complete verbless exchange about age.

chapters.title: Numbers 11–20 and Weather
chapters.label: ch:te-numbers-and-weather
chapters.canDo: I can say what the weather is doing in Telugu and count past ten up to twenty.

payoff.summary: Say వాతావరణం — a pure Sanskrit vāta + āvaraṇa, "the covering of air" — and report the weather with వర్షం పడుతోంది, "rain is falling."

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:te-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say కుక్క, which genuinely breaks from the family's shared naayi root, and పిల్లి, most likely the Dravidian source behind Hindi's billī.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:te-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can name green and yellow in Telugu, on top of the four colours I already had.

payoff.summary: Say పచ్చ and పసుపు and show they are doublets of one Proto-Dravidian \*pac- root — where Kannada's yellow broke away as a Sanskrit loan.

chapters.title: Day
chapters.label: ch:te-day
chapters.canDo: I can say "day" in Telugu and choose between the everyday Persian loan and its formal Sanskrit alternate.

payoff.summary: Say రోజు, a genuine Persian loan from rōz, and set it against the formal దినము — the mirror image of Kannada's plain dina.

chapters.title: Night
chapters.label: ch:te-night
chapters.canDo: I can say "night" in Telugu and recognise it inside the midnight word I already knew.

payoff.summary: Say రాత్రి, find it again inside అర్ధరాత్రి, and note the three native words — rēyi, māpu, irulu — it pushed aside.

chapters.title: Good Night
chapters.label: ch:te-good-night
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good night in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say శుభ రాత్రి — "auspicious night" — pairing the రాత్రి already learned with śubha, while knowing many speakers code-switch to English here.

chapters.title: Morning
chapters.label: ch:te-morning
chapters.canDo: I can say "morning" in Telugu with the same word that sits inside the morning greeting.

payoff.summary: Say ఉదయం, Telugu's broadest morning word, note the real native competitors poddu and vēkuva, and see that Kannada splits this job across two unrelated words.

chapters.title: Evening
chapters.label: ch:te-evening
chapters.canDo: I can say "evening" in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say సాయంత్రం, from sāyam plus a time-suffix, and follow its PIE \*seh₁- root across to Latin sērus, French soir and Italian sera.

chapters.title: Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:te-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can use Telugu's noon word to talk about the afternoon, and reach for the classical term when I need to be precise.

payoff.summary: Reuse మధ్యాహ్నం for the stretch between noon and evening, then contrast it with అపరాహ్నం, the more formal, more precise later-afternoon word.

chapters.title: Good Morning
chapters.label: ch:te-good-morning
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good morning in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say శుభోదయం — śubha + ఉదయం — and weigh the single low-authority claim that it is out of trend against నమస్కారం, the safer everyday bet.

chapters.title: Good Evening
chapters.label: ch:te-good-evening
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good evening in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Say శుభ సాయంత్రం, backed by two independent sources as genuinely common in both formal and casual speech, with నమస్కారం as an alternative rather than a replacement.

chapters.title: Good Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:te-good-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good afternoon in Telugu and judge whether it fits the setting I am in.

payoff.summary: Say శుభ మధ్యాహ్నం where the setting is formal or workplace-timed, and fall back on నమస్కారం, the time-independent everyday greeting.

chapters.title: The Core Verbs
chapters.label: ch:te-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can build a Telugu verb as stem plus tense plus person, say why one form covers both "I go" and "I will go", give a polite command with -aṇḍi, and explain why ఉండు has to borrow its negative and తెలుసు has no person at all.

payoff.summary: Say నాకు తెలుసు, name the three slots that built uṇṭānu, veḷtānu and cūstānu, separate it from Chapter 6's నాకు తెలుగు వచ్చు — fact against skill — and recall that ఉండు switches to lē- to be negated.

chapters.title: Four Verbs of the Mind
chapters.label: ch:te-verbs-of-the-mind
chapters.canDo: I can say I think, I understand, I read and I write in Telugu with the same three slots, build the -కో ending that hands an action back to its doer, say "I understood" with no నేను in it, and tell this chapter's native verbs from the Sanskrit words layered beside them.

payoff.summary: Say నేను తెలుగు రాస్తాను, run the chapter's four verbs in the present, count them up from ఆరు to పది, take వ్రాయు back to the Dravidian line-drawing root behind Tamil வரை and Kannada ಬರೆ, and name which of the four words came from Sanskrit.

chapters.title: Four Verbs Between People
chapters.label: ch:te-verbs-between-people
chapters.canDo: I can say I take, I ask and I help in Telugu, say నాకు తెలుగు ఇష్టం knowing there is no verb in it, place it beside the three other dative sentences I have built, and name the branch of Dravidian Telugu actually belongs to.

payoff.summary: Say నాకు తెలుగు ఇష్టం and unpack it as "to me, Telugu, a liking" with no verb at all; line it up against నాకు తెలుగు వచ్చు, నాకు తెలుసు and నాకు అర్థమైంది; choose between the native నచ్చు and ఇష్టపడు, whose పడు is the falling of వర్షం పడుతోంది; and trace ఇష్టం to the Indo-European root behind English ask.

chapters.title: Family and Friends
chapters.label: ch:te-family-and-friends
chapters.canDo: I can name my family as a group in Telugu and name a friend, and say which of the two words is a Sanskrit loan and which is Telugu's own native word.

payoff.summary: Say ఇది నా కుటుంబం and ఇతను నా స్నేహితుడు, trace కుటుంబం and స్నేహితుడు back to Sanskrit, and set స్నేహితుడు beside the native, DEDR-attested నేస్తం.

chapters.title: Son and Daughter, Two Different Roots
chapters.label: ch:te-son-and-daughter
chapters.canDo: I can say son and daughter in Telugu, and show that they trace to two different Proto-Dravidian roots rather than one shared root.

payoff.summary: Line up కొడుకు and కూతురు against their two separate Proto-Dravidian roots, trace కొడుకు's own root sideways to కోడలు ("daughter-in-law"), and trace కూతురు's root across the family to Kannada's word for infant.

chapters.title: Four Words on the Face
chapters.label: ch:te-face-words
chapters.canDo: I can name my eye, ear, nose and mouth in Telugu, and say which three the family agrees on and which one Telugu's word does not obviously match.

payoff.summary: Name కన్ను, చెవి, ముక్కు and నోరు; close the loop Chapter 32 left open on కన్ను; and say why నోరు, unlike the other three, shows no visible trace of the shared vాy root Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada all carry.

chapters.title: The Heart, Two Ways
chapters.label: ch:te-heart
chapters.canDo: I can name my heart in Telugu two ways, the everyday native word and the literary Sanskrit loan, and trace the Sanskrit one to the same Proto-Indo-European root as the English word heart.

payoff.summary: Say నా గుండె and నా హృదయం నీది, set the everyday native word beside the literary Sanskrit loan, and trace హృదయం to the same PIE root as English heart, Latin cor and Greek kardía.

chapters.title: Tea and Milk, Two Roads
chapters.label: ch:te-tea-and-milk
chapters.canDo: I can politely ask for tea or milk in Telugu, and say which word travelled by sea and which one three Dravidian cousins share under one regular sound law.

payoff.summary: Ask దయచేసి టీ and దయచేసి పాలు, follow టీ along its sea route through Hokkien and Malay against the overland chai route, then place పాలు beside Tamil and Malayalam's matching pāl against Kannada's own p-to-h shift.

chapters.title: A Meal
chapters.label: ch:te-a-meal
chapters.canDo: I can say I am having a meal in Telugu, using the word an earlier chapter already used and never explained.

payoff.summary: Say భోజనం చేద్దాం, explain భోజనం against everyday తిండి the way Chapter 32 first set them side by side, and apologise for a late meal with Chapter 9's క్షమించండి.

chapters.title: Pointing, and Asking
chapters.label: ch:te-pointing-and-asking
chapters.canDo: I can point at something in Telugu and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.

payoff.summary: Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.

chapters.title: Describing Things
chapters.label: ch:te-describing-things
chapters.canDo: I can point at something in Telugu and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.

payoff.summary: Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.

chapters.title: More Everyday Verbs
chapters.label: ch:te-more-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can tell someone to come, sit, stand and give in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Complete TE-C43-give and say all four verbs in order.

chapters.title: Verbs of Seeing and Saying
chapters.label: ch:te-see-say
chapters.canDo: I can tell someone to look, listen, speak and write in Telugu.

payoff.summary: Complete TE-C44-write and say all four verbs in order.

chapters.title: Grandparents, and the Married Pair
chapters.label: ch:te-grandparents
chapters.canDo: I can name four more family and people words in this language.

payoff.summary: Complete TE-C45-wife and say all four words in order.
